entries.title: A light-year measures distance
entries.answer: Light travels so quickly that in one second it can cover about 300,000 kilometers in empty space. But stars are so far apart that even light takes years to move between them. A light-year is the distance light travels in a whole year. When we see a star four light-years away, our eyes are receiving light that left it about four years ago. Looking deeper into space often means seeing farther back in time.
facts: One light-year is about 9.5 trillion kilometers.

questions.text: Where do the stars closest to Earth fit into our galaxy?
How does light travel to our eyes?
Which telescope records light from very distant galaxies?

entries.title: Asteroids, the rocks between planets
entries.answer: An asteroid is a rocky or metal-rich object that moves around the Sun. Many asteroids are found between Mars and Jupiter, in a wide area called the asteroid belt. It is mostly empty space. Asteroids have many shapes and sizes. Some look like loose piles of rocks held together by gravity. The dents on some planets and moons show that space rocks can hit other worlds. A small piece that happens to glow on its way through Earth’s atmosphere is making a meteor, the flash we call a shooting star.
facts: Most known asteroids orbit the Sun in the main asteroid belt.
Jupiter and Mars sit on opposite sides of the main asteroid belt.

questions.text: What makes a comet different from many asteroids?
Which small rocky planet has lots of craters?
Which giant planet is on the outer side of the asteroid belt?

entries.title: Callisto’s crater-covered surface
entries.answer: Pictures of Jupiter’s moon Callisto show round marks almost everywhere. Rocks and pieces of ice struck the surface long ago, leaving wide bowls called craters. A surface with so many surviving craters has probably changed less than one where later activity erased the marks. Callisto is the farthest from Jupiter of the four large moons Galileo observed. Spacecraft measurements suggest it may have a salty ocean under the frozen crust.
facts: The crater basin Valhalla has many rings around it.

questions.text: What kinds of objects leave impact craters?
Which big moon of Jupiter keeps remaking parts of its surface?
Which moon beside Callisto is even larger?

entries.title: Ceres, a dwarf planet in the asteroid belt
entries.answer: Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt. Among all its rocky bodies is Ceres, a round world much larger than its neighbors. Its own gravity helped pull it into a nearly round shape, but it shares its path around the Sun with many other objects. Ceres is a dwarf planet. Images from the Dawn spacecraft show pale patches in a big crater. Scientists found that these patches contain salts left by liquid rising from below.
facts: Ceres was first spotted in 1801.

questions.text: What are the much smaller neighbors of Ceres like?
Why do two objects in very different places have the same name for their type?
Which planet orbits just inside the asteroid belt?

entries.title: Earth, our home planet
entries.answer: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only place where we know life exists. Most of its surface is covered by water. A layer of gases called the atmosphere surrounds the planet. We breathe part of that mixture. Earth spins about once a day. When your part of Earth faces the Sun, it is daytime. When it faces away from the Sun, it is night. At the same time Earth travels around the Sun, completing one trip in about a year.
facts: Earth has one Moon.
Earth’s air is mostly nitrogen and oxygen.

questions.text: Why is July summer in some places and winter in others?
Why does Earth’s Moon seem to change shape?
What have scientists found about water on Mars?

entries.title: Enceladus, the moon that sprays ice
entries.answer: Ice covers the small moon Enceladus, but a salty ocean lies deep beneath it. Near the south pole, cracks release jets of water vapor and ice grains. Some grains fall back and coat the ground, and others escape into space. NASA’s Cassini spacecraft flew through the jets and measured their contents. That let scientists study some material from the moon’s interior without having to land and drill through the shell of ice.
facts: The jets supply ice grains to one of Saturn’s rings.

questions.text: What hints tell us an ocean may lie beneath Europa?
Which other moon of Saturn has liquid on its surface?
What else makes Saturn easy to spot in pictures?

entries.title: Europa’s hidden ocean
entries.answer: Europa looks like an ice-covered ball scratched with long lines. Scientists think much of the ice sits above a global ocean of salty water. They have not seen the water directly. Measurements from passing spacecraft and the way the icy surface is arranged help them work out what may be underneath. The pulls from Jupiter and other moons bend Europa slightly, which can make heat inside the moon even though its surface is very cold.
facts: No life has been found on Europa.

questions.text: Which other icy moon sends material from its ocean into space?
What happens when the bending warms a more rocky moon?
How does water move around in Earth’s ocean?

entries.title: Exoplanets, worlds around other stars
entries.answer: A planet beyond our solar system is called an exoplanet. Many circle stars much like our planets circle the Sun. A faraway planet is often too faint to see next to its bright star. One way to find it is to measure a tiny dip in the starlight when the planet crosses in front of the star. Repeated dips can show how long the planet takes to go around once. Other methods measure movement of the star itself.
facts: A dip in light is one clue, so scientists look for other ways to check it.

questions.text: Which space telescope can study light from some atmospheres?
How are planets arranged near our own star?
Why can an orbiting planet make its star wobble?

entries.title: Galaxies and the Milky Way
entries.answer: A galaxy is an enormous group of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity. Some galaxies have swirling arms, others look like smooth blobs, and some have no neat shape. We live inside a galaxy called the Milky Way. Our Sun is just one of its many stars. In a really dark place, you may see a pale band across the night sky. It is what part of the Milky Way looks like from inside it, with the light from many distant stars blending together.
facts: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy.
Light from some galaxies takes billions of years to reach us.

questions.text: Which star is nearest to us?
Which much smaller neighborhood is Earth in?
What pulls stars and other matter together?

entries.title: Ganymede, the largest moon
entries.answer: Ganymede goes around Jupiter and is the largest moon in our solar system. It is wider than the planet Mercury, although it has much less mass. Its surface has dark patches with many craters and brighter areas scored by grooves. Ganymede also makes its own magnetic field. That is unusual for a moon. Scientists think there may be a deep salty ocean between layers of ice far beneath the surface.
facts: A moon can be wider than a planet because those names describe what the objects orbit.

questions.text: How does the small planet Mercury compare with this moon?
How can a magnetic field affect things nearby?
Which neighboring moon has more old impact marks?

entries.title: How a solar eclipse works
entries.answer: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon crosses in front of the Sun as seen from part of Earth. The Moon’s shadow falls on a patch of Earth. People in the darkest part of the shadow can have a total eclipse, when the Moon appears to cover the Sun’s bright face for a short time. People nearby may see a partial eclipse, in which only a piece of the Sun is hidden. The Moon’s path is tilted, so it usually passes a little above or below the Sun in our sky at new moon.
facts: A partial eclipse and a total eclipse can happen in different places during the same event.
Never use ordinary sunglasses to look at the Sun during an eclipse. Ask a grown-up to help you use safe solar viewing glasses or an indirect viewer.

questions.text: What does new moon mean the rest of the time?
What is the object giving off the light?
Why is the ground usually dark at night?

entries.title: How a star grows into a red giant
entries.answer: A star like the Sun spends much of its life joining hydrogen in its center to make helium and give off energy. Eventually its center runs low on hydrogen. The star’s inner parts change, and its outer layers expand far beyond their old size. Those outer layers become cooler and can look red or orange, even though the star may give off more light overall. Astronomers call this larger stage a red giant.
facts: Our Sun is expected to become a red giant billions of years from now.

questions.text: How does the Sun make energy at the stage it is in now?
What is left behind when a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers?
What kind of cloud can lost outer layers form?

entries.title: How a whole star can leave a city-sized object
entries.answer: When some massive stars run out of fuel, their centers squeeze down and the outer material blows away. If the collapsed center survives without becoming a black hole, it may become a neutron star. It can pack more mass than the Sun into a space about as wide as a large city. A neutron star can spin rapidly and send out beams. If a beam sweeps over Earth, instruments may record very regular pulses.
facts: A neutron star detected by such repeating pulses is called a pulsar.

questions.text: What makes the outer layers explode into space?
What can happen if a collapsing star’s remnant cannot hold itself up?
What smaller kind of star can leave an Earth-sized remnant?

entries.title: How the northern and southern lights glow
entries.answer: An aurora can look like a glowing ribbon moving across a dark sky. Far above the ground, fast particles give energy to oxygen and nitrogen in Earth’s atmosphere. The gases then give off some of that energy as visible light. Earth’s magnetic field helps guide many of the particles toward regions near the two poles. That is why auroras are common at high latitudes. Larger disturbances can sometimes make them visible farther from the poles.
facts: Oxygen can make green and red light, while nitrogen can contribute blue or purple colors.

questions.text: What does the Sun send toward Earth?
Why do we see only some kinds of light?
How can Earth’s magnetic field affect a tool on the ground?

entries.title: Io, Jupiter’s volcanic moon
entries.answer: Io is a moon of Jupiter with hundreds of volcanoes. Some send gas and dust high above its surface. The energy comes from gravity: Jupiter pulls harder on the side of Io that is closer, stretching the moon a little. Nearby moons help keep Io’s path from becoming a perfect circle, so that stretching changes as it moves. This repeated squeezing warms the rock inside, a little like bending a strip of material back and forth.
facts: Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system.

questions.text: What lies beneath the icy shell of a neighboring moon?
What can erupt from a volcano on Earth?
Which giant planet pulls on Io?

entries.title: Jupiter, the biggest planet
entries.answer: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the biggest in our solar system. It is about eleven times as wide as Earth. It has cloud bands that wrap around it and a huge storm called the Great Red Spot. Jupiter is called a gas giant because most of it is hydrogen and helium. You could not land on solid ground like Earth’s surface there. Jupiter also has moons of its own. With a small telescope, you can often see four of its largest moons as little points of light.
facts: Jupiter has faint rings.
The Great Red Spot is a storm.

questions.text: Which other gas giant has easy-to-see rings?
What is different about a star made mostly of the same gases?
What gives a rocky planet like Mars its red color?

entries.title: Mars, the red planet
entries.answer: Mars looks red from far away because its dust and rocks contain a kind of iron that has rusted. Up close, the ground can also look brown, tan, or gold. Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. It has thin air, cold ground, two small moons, and a volcano named Olympus Mons. Robots sent from Earth have found signs that rivers and lakes existed there long ago. They study the rocks and soil to find out what Mars used to be like.
facts: The two Martian moons are Phobos and Deimos.
Mars is about half as wide as Earth.

questions.text: How does Mars compare with our own planet?
Is rusty dust the same thing as Jupiter’s red spot?
How can melted rock build a mountain?

entries.title: Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun
entries.answer: Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system and the closest one to the Sun. Its rocky ground is covered in round dents called craters. These formed when space rocks struck the surface. Mercury goes around the Sun in just 88 Earth days, so it has the shortest year of any planet. It spins slowly, though, and daytime on a patch of ground can last a very long time. With hardly any gas around the planet to hold heat, the ground can get very hot in sunlight and very cold in darkness.
facts: Mercury has no moons.
Mercury’s surface has craters like the Moon’s.

questions.text: Why is Venus even hotter than Mercury?
Where do some of the rocks that leave craters come from?
How does the Sun heat a planet?

entries.title: Miranda’s cliffs and grooves
entries.answer: Miranda is one of the larger moons of Uranus, though it measures less than 500 kilometers across. Some parts of it have lots of round craters. Other parts are wrinkled into ridges and valleys that look as though different pieces of land were stitched together. Voyager 2 photographed these strange patterns as it passed Uranus. Scientists use the pictures to ask how the moon changed inside and underneath its icy surface.
facts: The first close pictures of Miranda came from Voyager 2 in 1986.

questions.text: Why does Miranda’s planet seem tipped on its side?
Which moon shows a very different landscape made mostly of craters?
What other worlds did Voyager 2 visit?

entries.title: Neptune, the farthest planet
entries.answer: Neptune is the eighth planet from the Sun, so a trip around the Sun takes about 165 Earth years. It is cold at the tops of its clouds, and powerful winds sweep across them. Neptune is an ice giant like Uranus. The name describes what it is made of, including large amounts of materials such as water and methane. It does not have a hard, icy ground to skate on. Astronomers found Neptune after working out that the pull of another planet could explain small changes in the path of Uranus.
facts: Triton is Neptune’s largest moon.
Neptune goes around the Sun more slowly than Earth does.

questions.text: What other ice giant tipped astronomers off about Neptune?
What tiny world usually travels farther out than Neptune?
How does gravity affect the path of something in space?

entries.title: Our solar system
entries.answer: The solar system is our Sun and everything held in orbit by its gravity. That includes eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, and smaller objects such as asteroids and comets. Starting closest to the Sun, the planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. The first four have rocky ground. The four beyond them are much bigger and have deep layers of gas. Earth travels around the Sun once a year. Each of the other planets has its own path and takes a different amount of time to make the trip.

sections.heading: One star among many
sections.text: The solar system is part of the Milky Way. Other stars in our galaxy have planets of their own.

facts: There is one star in our solar system: the Sun.
Neptune is the farthest of the eight planets from the Sun.

questions.text: What powers the star at the center of our solar system?
Which planet makes the quickest trip around the Sun?
Why is Pluto in a different group from the eight planets?
What is the Milky Way?

quiz.question: Which planet comes right after Earth if you travel away from the Sun?
quiz.explanation: Earth is third from the Sun. Mars is fourth.

entries.title: Phobos and Deimos, the moons of Mars
entries.answer: Phobos and Deimos are the two moons of Mars. They are both much smaller than Earth’s Moon and are shaped more like lumpy rocks than balls. Phobos is the bigger one and circles much closer to Mars. It moves around so quickly that from the ground it can appear to come up in the west and go down in the east. Deimos takes a little over a day to make one trip around Mars.
facts: Phobos has a large crater called Stickney.

questions.text: What would the ground under the two moons look like?
How can impacts change a moon’s surface?
What keeps even very small moons from drifting away?

entries.title: Saturn and its rings
entries.answer: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun. The wide rings around it are made of countless pieces of ice and rock. Some pieces are as small as specks of dust. The pieces look like smooth bands from a distance, but each piece moves around Saturn on its own path. There are gaps between some bands. Saturn itself is a big planet made mainly of the gases hydrogen and helium. Just like Jupiter, Saturn has no rocky surface where you could stand.
facts: Saturn takes about 29 Earth years to go around the Sun.
The main rings are very thin compared with their width.

questions.text: What makes Jupiter another gas giant?
How can a planet spin on its side?
What keeps one object moving around another?

entries.title: The Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune
entries.answer: Beyond Neptune is a broad ring-shaped region called the Kuiper Belt. Countless bodies of ice and rock go around the Sun there. They are bits of the material left when the planets formed. Pluto is one of the largest known objects in the belt. After flying past Pluto, the New Horizons spacecraft passed a much smaller body named Arrokoth, which looks like two flattened snowballs joined together. Most objects in the belt have never been photographed so closely.
facts: Arrokoth’s two lobes were probably joined gently in the early solar system.

questions.text: How did Pluto become the best-known world in this region?
Which planet lies just inside much of the belt?
What happens when some icy bodies get close to the Sun?

entries.title: The Sun, our nearest star
entries.answer: The Sun is a star close enough to warm our planet and light up the daytime sky. Other stars can look like tiny dots because they are so far away. Deep inside the Sun, small pieces of atoms join to make larger ones. This process, called nuclear fusion, gives off energy. Some of that energy reaches us as light. The Sun is huge compared with Earth. Its gravity keeps Earth and the other planets moving around it instead of drifting off into space.
facts: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
Hydrogen and helium make up most of the Sun.

questions.text: What objects travel around the Sun?
Why does the Moon sometimes get in the way of sunlight?
Where is the Sun in the bigger universe?

entries.title: Titan, a moon with lakes
entries.answer: Titan is Saturn’s biggest moon. It has a thick atmosphere made mostly of nitrogen. Clouds and rain carry liquid around on Titan, but its surface is far too cold for ordinary liquid water. The rain and the lakes there contain methane and other substances that remain liquid in that cold. Water ice takes the place of much of the rock we see on Earth. A small spacecraft landed through Titan’s orange haze in 2005.
facts: Titan has rivers and lakes made of liquids other than water.

questions.text: How does water travel between air and land on Earth?
Which planet would fill much of the sky from Titan?
How does another Saturn moon bring hidden water up to space?

entries.title: Triton, the moon that orbits backward
entries.answer: Triton, Neptune’s biggest moon, goes around Neptune in the opposite direction from the way the planet spins. This makes scientists think Neptune may have caught Triton after it had orbited the Sun on its own. Triton’s surface is extremely cold, and part of its ice is frozen nitrogen. When Voyager 2 flew past in 1989, it photographed dark material rising in plumes that stretched into long streaks across the bright ground.
facts: The same face of Triton generally points toward Neptune throughout its orbit.

questions.text: What kind of planet captured Triton?
Where do many small icy worlds circle the Sun?
Which mission photographed Triton up close?

entries.title: Uranus, the planet on its side
entries.answer: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun. If Earth’s spin looks a bit like a tilted spinning top, the spin of Uranus looks more like that of a rolling wheel. Its axis, the line about which it turns, points almost sideways compared with most planets. That gives Uranus very long seasons as it travels around the Sun. Like Neptune, Uranus is called an ice giant. Deep inside it are materials that form familiar kinds of ice in colder places, even though they are very hot and squashed together inside the planet.
facts: A year on Uranus lasts about 84 Earth years.
Uranus has rings, though they are much fainter than Saturn’s.

questions.text: How does Earth’s smaller tilt cause seasons?
Which other planet is an ice giant?
Why can we see Saturn’s rings more easily?

entries.title: Venus, the hottest planet
entries.answer: Venus is the second planet from the Sun, almost the same size as Earth. Its air is mostly a gas called carbon dioxide. This thick layer slows the loss of heat to space, so Venus has a hotter surface than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun. Venus is wrapped in clouds that hide its ground from ordinary cameras. It shines brightly in our sky because those clouds reflect sunlight. Venus can appear near the horizon before sunrise or after sunset, depending on where it is in its trip around the Sun.
facts: Venus spins in the opposite direction from Earth.
Venus has no moons.

questions.text: What is it like on the planet closer to the Sun?
How is Earth different from Venus?
What lights both Venus and Earth?

entries.title: What are the Moon’s dark patches?
entries.answer: The large dark patches you see on the Moon are plains made of solid rock. Long ago, huge impacts made low basins, and later lava filled some of them. When the lava cooled it left broad areas of darker rock, often smoother than the high, bright land around them. Early people looking through telescopes called the areas seas. The old name remains even though close views and rock samples show what the patches are really made of.
facts: The Apollo 11 landing site was on a dark plain named the Sea of Tranquility.

questions.text: Who first collected rocks from a dark lunar plain?
What forms when lava cools and hardens on Earth?
Why are the near-side dark patches so familiar to us?

entries.title: What blows outward from the Sun?
entries.answer: The Sun’s very hot outer atmosphere sends a flow of tiny particles into space. This flow is called the solar wind, but it is not a wind made of ordinary air like the wind on Earth. The particles carry electric charges and interact with magnetic fields. Earth’s magnetic field changes the paths of many of them. The solar wind spreads beyond the planets, forming a large region where the Sun’s influence is important.
facts: The Voyager spacecraft have traveled beyond the main bubble formed by the solar wind.

questions.text: How can this flow help make northern lights?
How did a spacecraft study the wind closer to its beginning?
Which explorers traveled outside the Sun’s particle bubble?

entries.title: What is a nebula?
entries.answer: A nebula is a great cloud in space, made of gas, dust or both. Some clouds contain pockets where gravity draws material together until a new star can form. Other clouds are material a star has blown off or thrown out. A nearby star may light up part of a cloud. Dust in front of bright stars can also make a nebula look like a dark patch, even though there is material in that patch.
facts: A nebula can be both a place where stars start and a sign that stars have changed.

questions.text: How can a star send some of its outer material back to space?
What kind of explosion leaves a spreading cloud behind?
How can infrared light help us see into dusty places?

entries.title: What makes a star explode as a supernova?
entries.answer: A supernova is an explosion that can make a star suddenly extremely bright. One kind happens when a very massive star’s center collapses and a blast sends much of the rest of the star outward. Another kind involves a white dwarf in a pair of stars. The spreading gas can carry material from inside the star into space, where it may eventually mix with clouds that form new stars and planets.
facts: The Sun is not massive enough to explode by the first process.

questions.text: What can remain at the center after some explosions?
How can the spreading gas become a cloud that telescopes can see?
What ending is more likely for a star like our Sun?

entries.title: What remains when a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers?
entries.answer: When a star close to the Sun’s size reaches its final stages, it can send its outer layers drifting away. The very dense center left behind is called a white dwarf. It can have a lot of mass even though it is about the size of Earth. It does not rely on ordinary star fusion to keep glowing. Instead it slowly cools, like something once hot that takes a very long time to lose its warmth.
facts: A cloud around a newly exposed white dwarf can glow when lit by the hot remnant.

questions.text: What happens to the star before its center is exposed?
What much smaller remnant can a more massive star leave?
How can warmth leave a hot object in otherwise empty space?

entries.title: Where are we in the Milky Way?
entries.answer: The Sun is one star in a huge disk of stars called the Milky Way. If you could look down on that disk from well above it, you would see a long bar of stars in the middle and spiral arms curving around it. Our solar system sits far outside the bar in a smaller branch called the Orion Spur. As the planets circle the Sun, that whole solar system also travels around the center of the galaxy.
facts: The Sun’s path around the galaxy is much longer than any planet’s orbit around the Sun.

questions.text: Do other galaxies all have this shape?
How do planets move within our tiny part of the Milky Way?
How do astronomers describe such enormous distances?

entries.title: Where very long-traveling comets may come from
entries.answer: Some comets pass the Sun once and may take thousands of years to return. Scientists think many begin in a vast outer region called the Oort Cloud. It may surround the solar system roughly like a ball-shaped shell rather than a flat belt. Small ice-rich bodies there are too far away and dark for us to see well. A tiny tug from a passing star or the gravity of the galaxy can send one toward the Sun.
facts: Astronomers inferred the Oort Cloud from the paths of comets instead of seeing a whole cloud directly.

questions.text: How is a belt of nearby icy worlds shaped differently?
What happens to the ice after a comet warms near the Sun?
Where does this proposed cloud fit around the planets?

entries.title: Which pieces of space rock reach the ground?
entries.answer: Many bits of space rock heat up during their fast trip into Earth’s air. They can make a streak of light called a meteor. Most small pieces break apart or are used up high overhead. If a fragment reaches the ground, the remaining object is called a meteorite. In a museum, you may see a meteorite with a dark crust on the outside. Its inside can tell scientists what the original object contained.
facts: Some meteorites found on Earth originally came from the Moon or Mars.

questions.text: Why do many smaller bits sometimes arrive together?
Where do many rocky bodies circle the Sun?
Why collect a sample directly from an asteroid if rocks already fall here?

entries.title: Why comets grow tails
entries.answer: A comet is a small body of ice, dust, and rock that travels around the Sun. When a comet comes into warmer parts of the solar system, some of its ice changes straight into gas. The gas and dust spill into space and form a fuzzy cloud. Light from the Sun and a stream of particles from the Sun push material away, forming tails. A comet’s tails can point away from the Sun even when the comet itself is heading away from the Sun too.
facts: The solid center of a comet is called its nucleus.
Comets may have separate tails of gas and dust.

questions.text: What do asteroids contain instead of lots of ice?
What provides the energy that warms a comet?
What other icy world lives in the outer solar system?

entries.title: Why dark spots appear on the Sun
entries.answer: Some parts of the Sun are held by strong magnetic fields. Those fields can reduce the motion that normally carries heat up from below. A cooler area may then appear darker than the hotter material next to it. These dark-looking areas are called sunspots. A sunspot is still hot and gives off a lot of light. The number and locations of sunspots change over time as the Sun’s magnetic activity changes.
facts: A dark-looking sunspot would still shine brightly against empty space.

questions.text: Where does the Sun get the energy that moves out toward its surface?
How can activity at the Sun affect conditions far away?
What spacecraft can get close to the Sun’s outer atmosphere?

entries.title: Why Earth has seasons
entries.answer: Earth has seasons because the line it spins around is tilted. During part of the year, the northern half leans toward the Sun. Sunlight reaches it more directly, and the days are longer, so it has summer. The southern half gets less direct sunlight and shorter days, so it has winter. About six months later, the halves switch roles. That is why you might wear a thick coat in Boston in January while people in Sydney, Australia, are in the middle of summer.
facts: The tilt of Earth’s axis is about 23 degrees.
Earth’s North and South Poles each have long stretches of daylight or darkness.

questions.text: What motion gives Earth its days and nights?
How are seasons different on a planet that spins sideways?
How is climate different from one hot or cold day?

entries.title: Why light cannot escape a black hole
entries.answer: A black hole is a place where so much mass is packed into a small region that, past a certain boundary, nothing can get back out. This boundary is the event horizon. It traps even light, so a black hole itself does not shine. Astronomers can study one by tracking nearby stars, or by detecting light from hot gas outside the boundary. A black hole does not scoop up everything around it. Faraway things can orbit it.
facts: Some black holes form after a massive star runs out of fuel and its center collapses.

questions.text: What makes objects pull on one another in the first place?
Where are many of the heaviest black holes found?
How can light from near a black hole tell us about the distant past?

entries.title: Why many meteors can appear on one night
entries.answer: A meteor is the bright streak we see when a small piece of material enters Earth’s air very fast. At certain times of year, Earth crosses trails of dust left by comets. Many bits enter the air on the same night, making a meteor shower. They may seem to spread out from one spot in the sky, even though they travel on nearly parallel paths. It is like looking along straight rows of trees that seem to meet in the distance.
facts: A shower often returns around the same dates because Earth passes the trail on its yearly trip around the Sun.

questions.text: What happens if a piece is big enough to reach the ground?
How do comets leave loose dust behind?
Where else can small objects that enter our air come from?

entries.title: Why Pluto is a dwarf planet
entries.answer: Pluto is a small world of rock and ice that goes around the Sun. It is round like a planet, but its gravity does not control its path’s neighborhood. Pluto shares that area with many other objects, and Neptune’s pull helps shape Pluto’s path. That is one difference between a dwarf planet and one of the eight planets. Pluto also has moons of its own. In 2015 a spacecraft called New Horizons flew past Pluto and showed us its mountains, plains, and a huge bright area shaped a little like a heart.
facts: Pluto takes about 248 Earth years to orbit the Sun.
Pluto’s biggest moon is Charon.

questions.text: Which of the eight planets is Pluto’s near neighbor?
What other icy objects travel around the Sun?
How do all eight planets fit into the solar system?

entries.title: Why some days are longer than others
entries.answer: Earth’s axis is tilted as our planet travels around the Sun. Around the June solstice, the north half leans most toward the Sun and has its longest days. The south half has its shortest days. Around each equinox, neither half leans toward the Sun, so days and nights are nearly the same length in many places. Later in the year, the north half tilts away while the south half enjoys its longest days.
facts: The solstices generally occur in June and December, and the equinoxes in March and September.

questions.text: How does a change in the Sun’s angle affect temperatures?
Why does how far north or south you live change your summer daylight?
How can an orbiting satellite record the changing daylight pattern from space?

entries.title: Why the Moon can turn red during an eclipse
entries.answer: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the Sun and the full Moon so that the Moon moves through Earth’s shadow. In a total eclipse, most direct sunlight is blocked from reaching it. Some sunlight still bends through the air around Earth’s edge. The air scatters much of the blue light out of this path, leaving red and orange light to reach the Moon. We see that light reflect back.
facts: Most full moons miss Earth’s shadow because the Moon’s path is slightly tilted.

entries.title: Why the Moon changes shape in the sky
entries.answer: The Moon is always round, even when it looks like a thin slice. Usually, sunlight lights up one half of the Moon. As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of that bright half. A full moon shows almost all of it. A new moon happens when the lit half mostly faces away from us. The changing views are called the Moon’s phases. They repeat about every month. Earth’s shadow causes a lunar eclipse, which is a separate event from the usual phases.

sections.heading: Where to see a full moon
sections.text: Around full moon, the Moon rises roughly when the Sun sets. They look nearly opposite each other in the sky.

facts: We can sometimes see the Moon in daylight.

entries.title: Why the Moon keeps the same face toward Earth
entries.answer: The Moon spins once during each trip around Earth. Because the two motions take the same time, nearly the same side stays pointed toward us. Imagine walking in a circle around a table while always facing the person in the middle. Your body turns once even though that person keeps seeing your front. The Moon’s far side is not always dark. Sunlight falls on different parts of the Moon during each month.
facts: A far-side photograph shows places people cannot see directly from Earth.
